claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles can exhibit enhanced structural and chemical stability at elevated service temperatures.
Local lattice distortions create kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
Short-range chemical ordering creates kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
Diffusion barriers produced by lattice distortion and short-range ordering delay phase separation at elevated temperature.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, disordered, single-phase, near-equiatomic solid solutions.
The initial nanoparticles possess inherent local lattice distortions.
The initial nanoparticles have statistically random elemental distributions.
A fabrication route can be selected that produces stronger local lattice distortions than the control route.
Local strain fields caused by lattice distortions raise the activation energy for atomic diffusion.
Phase separation and elemental segregation are thermodynamically favored at elevated temperatures in the proposed systems.
Kinetic trapping prevents or delays thermodynamically favored phase separation and elemental segregation.
Nanoparticles with pronounced local distortions will retain a single-phase homogeneous microstructure and uniform elemental distribution after annealing at 773–1173 K.
Control nanoparticles with minimized lattice distortions will exhibit phase separation and chemical segregation earlier than strongly distorted nanoparticles under identical thermal treatment.
The proposed kinetic stabilization mechanism operates primarily between 773 and 1173 K.
At substantially higher temperatures or sufficiently long annealing durations, kinetically trapped nanoparticles may eventually phase-separate.
Increasing local lattice distortion also promotes short-range chemical ordering.
